entities.name: Yñigo Ortiz de Retez
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Yñigo Ortiz de Retez, a Spanish maritime explorer of Basque descent, etched his name into the annals of global exploration during the mid-16th century, specifically through his pivotal 1545 voyage that circumnavigated much of New Guinea's northern coast. Operating within the vast, ambitious framework of Spanish imperial expansion across the Pacific, Ortiz de Retez was not merely an intrepid navigator but a significant conduit for European geographical knowledge, contributing directly to the mapping of one of the world's largest and most enigmatic islands. His expedition, authorized by the Viceroy of New Spain, Antonio de Mendoza, aimed to solidify Spanish claims and locate potential trade routes and resources in the sprawling, largely uncharted Pacific realm, making him a figure at the confluence of early modern exploration, cartography, and nascent colonial ambition.

In May 1545, Ortiz de Retez departed from Tidore in the Moluccas aboard the carrack *San Juan*, under orders from Governor Villalobos, to explore the eastern reaches of the Spice Islands and beyond. After sailing north of Halmahera, he charted a course eastward, meticulously traversing over 1,000 kilometers of the previously unknown northern coastline of what is now New Guinea. During this arduous journey, which lasted from June 20 to August 19, 1545, Ortiz de Retez made the pivotal observation that the land's inhabitants bore a physical resemblance to the peoples of the Guinea coast in West Africa. This striking similarity prompted him to christen the island "Nueva Guinea" (New Guinea), a name that has persisted for nearly five centuries. His expedition also collected ethnographic details, observing the local populations and their distinct cultural practices, thereby expanding European understanding of Pacific societies, albeit through a colonial lens.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Yñigo Ortiz de Retez's 1545 expedition was regionally significant for officially naming New Guinea, permanently placing one of the world's largest islands on European maps and influencing subsequent centuries of exploration and colonial claims in the Pacific.
